summary: This standards-track document describes how to carry H.264 Scalable Video Coding (SVC) video in RTP packets. One video stream is encoded in layers, so receivers with weaker links or smaller screens can use just the layers they can handle. It explains how to pack and split the coded units across packets and how layers can be sent in one or several RTP sessions.

plainLanguage.summary:
Scalable video is one video file that contains several quality levels, so a weak network or a small screen can be given just the part it can use. This RFC describes how to carry that over RTP, the protocol that moves live video, and how the two ends agree on the details before the video starts.

Every piece of the video carries a label saying which layer it belongs to, so the receiver and any device in the middle can drop what is not needed.

subtitle: How scalable video is carried over RTP, so each viewer can take only the quality they can use.

tldr.problem: A scalable video bitstream holds the same video at several quality levels, and there was no agreed way to carry it over RTP or to tell the two ends what to send.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the H.264 payload format with an SVC NAL unit header that names the layer of every piece of the video, defines new packet structures for aggregation and for scaling information, and adds a media subtype with SDP parameters for the configuration.
tldr.outcome: One video can be sent in one session or several, and in a multicast session each receiver can take a different layer. The document is a Proposed Standard and builds on the H.264 payload format in RFC 6184.

today: RFC 6190 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the RTP payload format for Scalable Video Coding and the media subtype H264-SVC, and it builds on the payload format for plain H.264 video in RFC 6184. Its dependency signalling follows the rules of RFC 5583.

sections.title: Carrying Scalable Video over RTP
sections.content:
Most video sent over the Internet today is coded with H.264/AVC. Scalable Video Coding extends it so that one bitstream holds the same video at several levels of quality, and a receiver can take only the part it can use. This document describes how that scalable bitstream is carried over RTP, the transport protocol that carries real-time media, and how a session is set up so that both ends agree on what is being sent.

The payload format is similar to the one for plain H.264 video defined in RFC 6184, and it follows the same design principles: backward compatibility where possible, so that the base layer of an SVC stream can be understood by an ordinary H.264 receiver, and a media-aware network element, which is a device in the middle that understands the media and can thin the stream, is allowed to aggregate several streams and to drop the parts a receiver does not need.

The memo also defines the signalling support for SVC over RTP, including a new media subtype name, H264-SVC.
sections.plainLanguage: Scalable video is one video file that contains several quality levels, so a weak network or a small screen can be given just the part it can use. This RFC describes how to carry that over RTP, the protocol that moves live video, and how the two ends agree on the details before the video starts.

sections.title: How SVC Builds a Scalable Video
sections.content:
SVC defines a coded video representation in which one bitstream offers the source material at different levels of fidelity, which is where the word scalable comes from. The bitstream is built in a pyramidal way: the coding process creates components that improve the fidelity of hierarchically lower components.

The fidelity has three dimensions. Spatial is the picture size, quality is the signal-to-noise ratio, and temporal is the number of pictures per second. The components at a given level are identified by three parameters in the bitstream: dependency_id for the spatial level, quality_id for the quality level and temporal_id for the frame rate. Higher values mean components that are higher in the hierarchy. How the encoder arranges the dependencies between components is left to it, but decoding a component needs every component it depends on, directly or indirectly. The set of components needed to decode one combination of the three identifiers is an operation point.

SVC keeps the bitstream organisation of H.264/AVC. All the components are carried in Network Abstraction Layer units, which are organised into Access Units, one per sampling instance in time. A subset of the NAL unit types, the Video Coding Layer ones, hold the coded picture data. The other NAL units carry data that may be needed for decoding, such as parameter sets, or that helps the system without being needed to decode.

SVC uses three NAL unit types that H.264/AVC had reserved. Type 14 is the prefix NAL unit, type 15 is the subset sequence parameter set, and type 20 is the coded slice in scalable extension, whose header carries the fidelity parameters. All three are ignored by decoders that conform to the H.264/AVC profiles.

Within one access unit, the Video Coding Layer NAL units with a given dependency_id and quality_id are called a layer representation. The one with both values at zero is by design compatible with H.264/AVC. The document uses the term AVC base layer for the base layer without the SVC-specific prefix NAL units, and SVC base layer for the same layer with them, and it uses T0 for the part of a layer with temporal_id zero.

Signal-to-noise scalability comes in two forms. Coarse-grain scalability provides it by including or leaving out a whole layer. Medium-grain scalability provides it by selectively leaving out particular NAL units of medium-grain layers, and the choice can be made from fixed-length fields in the NAL unit header.
sections.plainLanguage: The video is built in layers. Each layer adds something to the one below, and a layer cannot be decoded without the layers it depends on. Three numbers describe a layer: how big it is, how good it looks, and how many pictures per second it has.

sections.title: The SVC NAL Unit Header
sections.content:
SVC extends the one-byte H.264/AVC NAL unit header with three more octets, for NAL units of types 14 and 20. The header says what type the NAL unit is, whether the payload may contain bit errors or syntax violations, how important the unit is for decoding, the layer identification information, and a few other fields.

The first byte has the same three fields as in H.264/AVC. The forbidden_zero_bit is one bit, and H.264/AVC declares a value of 1 to be a syntax violation. The nal_ref_idc is two bits, and a value of 00 means the content is not used to rebuild reference pictures for future prediction, so the unit can be dropped without harming the reference pictures of the same layer. The nal_unit_type is five bits and names the type of the unit.

The three added octets carry the SVC fields. The reserved_one_bit is one bit and must be 1, and decoders must ignore it. The idr_flag says whether the layer representation is an instantaneous decoding refresh, which starts a new coded video sequence. The priority_id is six bits, and a lower value means a higher priority. The no_inter_layer_pred_flag says whether inter-layer prediction may be used for coding the slice. The dependency_id is three bits and gives the inter-layer dependency level, so a layer may be used to predict a higher dependency level but not a lower one. The quality_id is four bits and gives the quality level, where a layer with quality_id ql uses the layer with ql-1 for prediction. The temporal_id is three bits and gives the temporal level, where lower values mean lower frame rates, and a layer never depends on a higher temporal level. The use_ref_base_pic_flag says whether only reference base pictures are used in the inter prediction process. The discardable_flag says whether the unit is needed to keep the layers with a higher dependency_id intact. The output_flag affects the decoded picture output process, and the reserved_three_2bits are two bits that must be 11 and are ignored by decoders.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of the video carries a header. Three extra bytes say which layer it belongs to, how important it is, and whether it can be thrown away without breaking the layers above it.

sections.title: Transmission Modes and Packetization Modes
sections.content:
The memo allows SVC data to be carried in one RTP session, which is called single-session transmission, or in two or more, which is called multi-session transmission. In the single-session case all the SVC data go in one session; in the multi-session case each session carries one RTP stream, which may hold one or more layers.

Single-session transmission SHOULD be used for point-to-point unicast, and multi-session transmission SHOULD be used for a multicast session where different receivers may want different layers. The number of streams used should be at least the number of operation points the receivers may ask for, which may mean a separate stream per layer. The choice is made with the mst-mode media type parameter: if it is not present, single-session transmission MUST be used, and if it is present, multi-session transmission MUST be used.

An RTP stream may carry one of three layer combinations: the T0 AVC base layer or the T0 SVC base layer alone, one or more enhancement layers alone, or the T0 SVC base layer together with one or more enhancement layers. When an H.264/AVC compatible subset of the SVC base layer is sent in a single session, the packetization of RFC 6184 must be used, so that ordinary H.264 receivers understand it. When enhancement layers are sent, the packetization of this memo must be used.

Single-session transmission may use any of the three packetization modes of RFC 6184: single NAL unit mode, non-interleaved mode and interleaved mode. Multi-session transmission uses four modes defined here: non-interleaved timestamp based mode, NI-T; non-interleaved cross-session decoding order number mode, NI-C; non-interleaved combined timestamp and CS-DON mode, NI-TC; and interleaved CS-DON mode, I-C. The modes differ in whether the NAL units have to be sent within a certain time and in how the decoding order is recovered across sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The video can go in one session or several. One session is simpler and fits a call between two computers. Several sessions let each viewer in a multicast group pick a different quality, because each session can hold a different part of the video.

sections.title: The RTP Payload Structures
sections.content:
The payload format carries the raw NAL unit stream over RTP. It cannot carry the bytestream format of Annex B of H.264.

RFC 6184 defines three payload structures: the single NAL unit packet, the aggregation packet and the fragmentation unit, and it uses NAL unit types 1 to 23 for a single NAL unit packet, 24 to 27 for an aggregation packet, and 28 and 29 for a fragmentation unit. This memo adds three more NAL unit types: the PACSI NAL unit, type 30; the empty NAL unit, type 31 with subtype 1; and the NI-MTAP, type 31 with subtype 2.

Each RTP packet payload is still structured as a NAL unit, which holds one NAL unit or part of one, or one PACSI NAL unit or one empty NAL unit, or aggregates zero or more NAL units, zero or one PACSI NAL unit and zero or more empty NAL units. The length of the payload header depends on the type: four bytes when the type is 14, 20 or 30, two bytes when it is 31, and one byte otherwise.

The NI-MTAP is an aggregation packet that groups NAL units of different time instances in decoding order, which is what multi-session transmission needs. Each unit in it carries a timestamp offset, and the offset of the earliest unit MUST be zero, so the RTP timestamp of the NI-MTAP is the timestamp of the earliest unit.

The PACSI NAL unit carries information about the layers a packet depends on, so that a receiver or a network element can tell what would be lost by dropping it, and it is also used to recover the decoding order across sessions. Its first four octets are the same as the four-byte SVC NAL unit header, then come one octet of flags, five optional octets and zero or more SEI NAL units, each preceded by a 16-bit size field. When a PACSI NAL unit is inside an aggregation packet, it MUST be the first aggregated unit, there MUST be at least one other unit, and the headers of the packet are set as if the PACSI unit were not there.

Multi-session transmission also needs a way to recover the decoding order across sessions, and the memo defines a Decoding Order Number for that, with a cross-session form for multi-session transmission. There is also an empty NAL unit, used as filler.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP packets come in a few shapes. One holds a single piece of the video, one holds several pieces, and one holds a piece that was too big for a single packet. This RFC adds shapes for grouping pieces of different frames together, and for telling the receiver which layers a packet depends on.

sections.title: The Media Type and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The media type is video with the subtype H264-SVC, and it has no required parameters. The optional parameters describe the stream and the receiver's capabilities. profile-level-id gives the profile and level of the stream as three bytes taken from the sequence parameter set or the subset sequence parameter set. packetization-mode selects which of the packetization modes is in use, and mst-mode selects the multi-session mode. max-recv-level and max-recv-base-level say how much the receiver can take, and scalable-layer-id names the layer the receiver wants when it can only take one.

The sprop- parameters describe the stream: the parameter sets, how much buffering the receiver needs, how deeply the sender interleaves, the largest difference in decoding order numbers, the remultiplexing buffer, and the operation point information.

The parameters that state a receiver's capability are in general downgradable: they express an upper limit, and a sender MAY choose lower or equal values. The parameters that declare a configuration point are not changeable, except for the level part of profile-level-id in unicast use, and if level downgrading is used the answerer MUST NOT include scalable-layer-id. It is often advisable to offer several alternative configurations, but a payload type can hold only one, so each offer needs its own payload type. An answer MUST NOT contain a payload type number used in the offer unless the configuration is the same as in the offer.

In multi-session transmission, the dependency signalling rules of RFC 5583 apply, and the order of the dependencies given by the depend attribute MUST represent the decoding order of the Video Coding Layer NAL units in an access unit, from the base or lowest enhancement session to the highest.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree on the details in the session description. Some parameters say what the stream is, some say what the receiver can handle, and some say how the pieces are packed into packets. The receiver can lower a limit it announced, but the packing mode has to be exactly what was agreed.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
The congestion control rules of RFC 6184 apply to each RTP session carrying this payload. The bitrate of a session can be reduced in several ways. Within the highest layer named by the dependency_id, NAL units with a quality_id above a chosen value can be removed. NAL units with a temporal_id above a chosen value can be removed. NAL units associated with a dependency_id above a chosen value can be removed, and removing all the coded slice NAL units with dependency identifiers above a value across the whole stream is required to keep the resulting stream conforming.

The priority_id field can be used to say how important a unit is and remove the ones above a chosen value, though the use of that field is application specific. Or units or whole packets can be removed by rules of the application, which will generally leave a bitstream that does not conform, so the behaviour of the decoder is not specified, and artefacts may appear if the decoder does not react to the congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network gets tight, the sender can throw away the top layers of the video, and the header fields say which ones those are, so the receiver still gets something watchable.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the RTP payload format for H.264 video, RFC 6184, apply. Decoders MUST be careful with reserved NAL unit types and reserved SEI messages, particularly if they contain active elements, and MUST restrict their applicability to the presentation that contains the stream. The safest thing is to discard them.

When integrity protection is applied to a stream, care MUST be taken, because the stream may be scalable and a receiver may be able to access only part of the whole stream.

End-to-end protection, whether authentication, integrity or confidentiality, stops a media-aware network element from doing anything except dropping whole packets, and with confidentiality it stops it even from dropping packets in a media-aware way. To let such an element work, it has to be a trusted party that is part of the security context, on the media path and on the RTCP path if RTCP packets have to be rewritten.
sections.plainLanguage: Protecting the whole stream from end to end also stops a device in the middle from thinning it, so such a device has to be trusted to see the media.

viz.caption: THE THREE EXTRA OCTETS OF THE SVC NAL UNIT HEADER

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be 1 and ignored by decoders.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: idr_flag. 1 means the layer representation starts a new coded video sequence.

fields.name: PRID
fields.desc: priority_id. A lower value means a higher priority.

fields.name: N
fields.desc: no_inter_layer_pred_flag. Says whether inter-layer prediction may be used.

fields.name: DID
fields.desc: dependency_id. The inter-layer dependency level of the layer representation.

fields.name: QID
fields.desc: quality_id. The quality level; a layer with ql predicts from the layer with ql-1.

fields.name: TID
fields.desc: temporal_id. The temporal level; lower values mean lower frame rates.

fields.name: U
fields.desc: use_ref_base_pic_flag. Says whether only reference base pictures are used in prediction.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: discardable_flag. Says whether the unit can be dropped without harming higher layers.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: output_flag. Affects the decoded picture output process.

fields.name: RR
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be 11 and ignored by decoders.

items.title: Single NAL unit packet
items.text: One NAL unit, or part of one, in an RTP packet. Types 1 to 23, 30, and 31 with subtype 1.

items.title: Aggregation packet
items.text: Several NAL units in one RTP packet. Types 24 to 27, and 31 with subtype 2.

items.title: Fragmentation unit
items.text: A large NAL unit split over several RTP packets. Types 28 and 29.

items.title: PACSI NAL unit
items.text: Type 30. Says which layers the packet depends on and helps recover the decoding order.

items.title: Empty NAL unit
items.text: Type 31 with subtype 1. Used as filler.

messages.label: Enhancement layer
messages.note: Only if this receiver subscribed to it.
